extracted.intended_audience: unemployment insurance administrators, benefit control officers (BCOs), UIC supervisors, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Operational and legal guidance for initiating, conducting, and supervising unemployment insurance benefit-control investigations, including types of investigations, powers, interview technique, and procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: BCO job description — four areas of activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Benefit Control Officer's job description includes four areas of activity: investigations of specific individual cases; appearing on behalf of the UIC in criminal proceedings against claimants or employers; investigations of a particular category of claimants (high-incidence categories); and maintaining working relationships with other government departments and agencies to assist investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of category investigations include married female claimants between ages 25–35 and claimants with minimum weeks of insurable employment. BCOs must work with welfare agencies, Department of National Revenue, the courts, and other UIC branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical considerations and public role
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefit control raises ethical questions about the role of the public and officials — balancing awareness of social realities and financial insecurity of unemployment against duty to taxpayers; whether law‑abiding citizens must act as informers even when disclosure may harm needy claimants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the dilemma between preventing abuse and avoiding harm to claimants dependent on benefits; the issue arises in practice and should inform conduct and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment/background considerations for BCOs
rubrics_metrics.description: High proportion of BCOs are recruited from former policemen, private detectives and commercial collection investigators — this brings legal/investigative experience but may risk importing contested private-agency ethics and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both advantages (criminal investigation knowledge, practical procedures) and disadvantages (risk of tainting UIC operations with criticized private methods) when hiring or assigning duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation types — formal investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal investigations are the standard control operation, aimed at checking suspected irregularities or fraud and collecting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal investigations are initiated at the request of an Agent II in cases such as: discovery in the file suggesting fraud; Record of Employment raising voluntary leaving vs dismissal for misconduct; CMC alerts; or third-party reports of fraud. When requested, Benefit Control Unit receives documentation and Agent II must decide on preventive withholding (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation types — selective investigations (on‑premises and field)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective investigations aim to accomplish general benefit‑control objectives (check entitlement under sec.54(1), gather evidence, notify/remind claimants of obligations) and are not initiated by a specific file item or Agent II examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any claimant with a certain 'seniority' (e.g., drawn benefits ≥10 weeks) may be selected. Geographic criteria allocate cases to on‑premises (interview at office; excludes those beyond $3.00 return transport) or field investigations (interview/outside enquiries). Supervisors select cases weekly from Regional Pay Centre lists guided by local statistics and incidence factors (e.g., married women 25–35, male non-unionized workers 19–35, general labourers, those with in‑demand skills who nevertheless failed to find work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation types — post‑audit investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Post‑audit investigations determine whether a claimant had earnings during the benefit period that were unreported or incorrectly reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key document is the employer's Record of Employment (ROE). UIC extracts employment periods and earnings from the ROE and matches with benefit payment files; matching may only indicate a potential overpayment and requires requesting precise weekly earnings from employer and employee. If overpayment established, consider penalty and initiate collection action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation types — auxiliary investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary investigations are carried out by a Benefit Control Unit at the request of another District Office, generally due to claimant's change of address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedurally simple and of no particular special procedure interest; handled on request from other districts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation types — special investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Special investigations cover various questions without a predetermined procedure and can take forms such as random-sample file checks, forgery investigations, Social Insurance Number (SIN) misuse, or employer refusal to deliver/complete ROE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: investigations of forged signatures or altered cheques (possible police referral/prosecution); SIN investigations initiated by employers, immigration authorities, police, press, individuals, or head office; employer-ROE refusal may require seizure of employer accounts (see sec.73 powers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisor decision on justifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: When a request for investigation is received, the Benefit Control Unit supervisor must decide whether the investigation is justifiable, particularly in terms of expected savings/recovery relative to investigation costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not justifiable, return the request with comments. If justifiable, ensure all necessary documentation and information are present before assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive withholding of benefits standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An Agent II must decide whether to withhold benefits pending investigation; benefits should only be suspended when there are serious indications that benefits are being paid unlawfully and when the suspected abuse is continuous/repeated rather than an isolated incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid suspension for cases likely to be 'par for the course'; in practice Agents II sometimes suspend payments, but standard is serious indication + continuity of abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment and mix of investigation types to BCOs
rubrics_metrics.description: The supervisor of the Benefit Control Unit assigns a mix of all types of investigations to each BCO in his unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervisors must balance workloads and types; BCOs may prefer more control over assigned work and can feel encumbered by requests they view as of little use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of cases between support staff and BCOs
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases with small amounts or where the claimant admits incorrect reporting may be handled by Benefit Control support staff without BCO involvement; cases with substantial potential overpayments are handled by the BCO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dividing line varies depending on volume of post‑audit cases and other workload; supervisors set thresholds in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal powers under sec.73 and sec.113 (entry, documents, questions, sanctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sec.73 (and sec.122(2) linkage) authorizes BCOs to enter premises to audit deductible/payment of premiums, obtain assistance from document holders, seize documents if evidence of an offence exists, require persons to furnish information or produce documents (by registered letter or personal demand), and make copies. Sec.113 empowers officers to enter premises where persons are or were employed to make inquiries necessary to determine entitlement. Failure or obstruction and false/misleading information constitute offences (secs.121, 122, 123, 124), with fines/imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UIC delegates exercise of these powers to BCOs; these coercive powers are circumscribed in statute to legitimize and avoid abuse. Sec.14(1) and sec.113(3) authorize receiving statements under oath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum coercion principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite statutory coercive powers, the BCO's day-to-day job is to obtain the maximum amount of information for benefit control with the minimum amount of coercion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As far as possible, BCOs should obtain claimants' co‑operation and attempt to interview claimants rather than rely on coercive measures or questionnaires sent by mail (used only exceptionally).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview location guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews are to be on UIC premises unless there is evidence that a field investigation or residence interview is necessary to establish the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field/residence interviews appropriate when on‑premises success doubtful: claimant failed to report for office interview, suspected self‑employed, suspected to have found work, or rural/remote areas. Use residence interviews cautiously to avoid intrusion/embarrassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑party presence policy at interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Since July 1975, UIC permits third parties at benefit control interviews only to advise/assist the claimant or act as an interpreter; third parties may not act as the claimant's representative (except interpreters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If third‑party presence makes a reasonable interview impossible, BCOs should agree on another interview date. Interpret presence narrowly to avoid third parties obstructing fact‑finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and disclosure in field interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: BCOs must identify themselves and the purpose of their visit when conducting field interviews; for interviews with third parties, discretion may be used regarding disclosure if revealing purpose would embarrass the claimant or third party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh need for transparency against potential embarrassment; apply discretion to avoid undermining investigation or causing undue harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to warn claimants about criminal implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether BCOs are required to warn claimants in advance of possible implications of their statements (criminal prosecution or effect on Agent II decision); UIC contends officers are not required to warn claimants because refusal to answer does not by itself create criminal liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UIC policy: no general warning requirement; exercise caution in practice given potential legal or fairness concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to attend interview
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimant fails to attend an interview arranged by UIC, the Agent II may disentitle the claimant under sec.54(1) and sec.55(6) of the Act; more extensive investigations may trigger use of Data Centre resources to locate claimants or contact recoveries sections for recidivists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BCOs should prioritize locating missing claimants and coordinate with central data and recovery units when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview conduct and psychological techniques (Training Guide)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Training Guide prescribes that investigators should have interest in human nature, quickly assess personalities, 'act the part convincingly', use changes in demeanour, voice, facial expression and speech rate as questioning techniques, but maintain complete self‑control and not permit genuine anger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dramatics intentionally, avoid emotional involvement, use a calculated display of annoyance to indicate jeopardy, be a 'good salesman' to undermine confidence of the subject and persuade witnesses to cooperate; high‑order salesmanship is required to obtain cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourteen commandments for investigators (interviewing principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of 14 explicit behavioural rules for investigators (Training Guide): e.g., 1. Subdue prejudices; 2. Keep an open mind; 3. Evaluate developments on merits; 4. Do not try to impress; 5. Tell the truth; 6. Do not underestimate subject; 7. Avoid contempt/ridicule; 8. Speak quietly unless raising voice for effect; 9. Avoid nervous signs; 10. Be a fact‑finder not a prosecutor; 11. Be dominant without domineering; 12. Be a good listener; 13. Be patient and persistent; 14. Do not preach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these as core interview ethics and tactics; formal questioning is described as a battle of wits to be conducted coolly, objectively, fairly, courteously, and without undue harshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening verification steps in interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: At the start of an interview, BCOs should verify the identity of the interviewee by asking for the Social Insurance Card and comparing the number and signature with those on the application for benefit; also ask claimant to verify authenticity of the application form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the claimant's file within reach to confirm items and confront the claimant with previous statements as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questioning technique and required topics for general control
rubrics_metrics.description: BCOs should encourage claimants to talk, limit their own interventions, and gather information sufficiently conclusive for the Agent II's decision. For general control, cover claimant's capability to work by asking about reasons for leaving employment, health when leaving or applying, work done since application, and chances/steps to be rehired by former employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt question types to nature of investigation (general control vs suspected specific issue) but maintain the goal of equipping Agent II with all pertinent facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mail/questionnaires only in exceptional remote cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication by mail (sending a questionnaire) is used only in exceptional cases for claimants in the most remote areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer interviews (office or field) to written questionnaires to obtain fuller information and reduce misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union hiring‑hall exemption criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimants who belong to unions that have organized a hiring hall and signed an 'umbrella agreement' with the UIC may be exempt from investigations concerning their job search during a specified period provided they use the hiring hall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To retain exemption, unions must satisfy UIC that they maintain hiring efficiency and allow UIC to examine records. Practice concentrated in major industrial centres (e.g., ~130 unions in metropolitan Toronto) and may not be widespread elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview scheduling priority
rubrics_metrics.description: When drawing up an interview schedule, BCOs should give priority to cases with urgency — cases involving suspected fraud have priority over simple control, and claimants whose benefit periods are continuing have priority over former claimants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where contact by telephone is possible, summon the claimant to interview within 24 hours unless circumstances require fieldwork or residence interview. Consider cases' urgency and continuity when allocating interview slots.
